# Playbook for Letter Auction

When I see the auction starting, I need to recognize that I'm playing against an opponent whose bids I won't see until after I commit. This means I should bid based on letter utility and strategic positioning, not on what happened before.

When a low-value letter (worth 1 point) comes up early, I should bid more aggressively than I did. However, I must also recognize that aggressive bidding on every vowel and common letter early will drain my coin reserves before the auction ends. S went for 5, A went for 5, E went for 5—I won E but only because I bid 5 while my opponent bid 0. This taught me that overbidding early leaves me broke midway through.

When I win a letter, I should immediately assess what words become possible with my growing collection. After Letter 3, I had only E and was already out of coins by Letter 6. This means I bid too much too fast and lost the ability to compete for remaining letters.

My mistake was not in bidding aggressively, but in bidding aggressively on letters where my opponent wasn't competing. I bid 5 on E when my opponent bid 0—I overpaid. I should bid at the minimum level needed to win against actual competition, not bid high against passive opposition.

When I have 12 coins and there are 8 letters to auction, I cannot afford to spend 3-5 coins per letter without running dry. I need to ration my coins: perhaps spend more on the letters most critical to my word-forming strategy, and bid 0 or 1 on letters my opponent seems uninterested in.

When multiple high-value letters (S, A, E—all essential vowels) appear in the first three slots, I should not try to win all of them. Instead, I should pick one or two key letters to contest and let my opponent overpay on the others. Then I preserve coins for mid-auction turns when I know what I'm building toward.

When a mid-value letter like M (worth 3) comes up, I should bid for it if my coin reserves allow. M enables high-scoring words like MASTER, STREAM, TAMER. But I should only pursue M if I've secured vowels first with coins remaining.

When I have coins remaining with several letters left to auction, I should not bid 0 automatically. I should bid for letters that complete high-value words. R enables STREAM, MASTER, TEARS—these are worth acquiring if I have the vowels to back them up.

When I reach the word-submission phase, the game is already decided by my auction performance. SEA scored 3 points (each letter worth 1), plus 0 unspent coins = 3. My opponent likely formed a longer, higher-value word because they acquired more letters. The damage is done at the auction stage.

Next time, I will:
- Spend selectively on early letters, not trying to win the first vowel offered
- Bid just enough to win against actual competition, not overpay against silence
- Preserve 6-8 coins for mid-to-late auction turns
- Focus on building one coherent word path (e.g., STREAM or MASTER) rather than scattered letters
- Let opponents overpay for early letters while I accumulate strategically

My final score of 6 (3 from SEA + 0 unspent coins) was poor because I bid away my ability to compete. Next game, I will bid like I have a fixed budget for specific letters, not like I should spend coins whenever a useful letter appears.

# Letter Auction Playbook

When I'm shown a letter to bid on, I need to recognize that my actual goal is to accumulate letters that form a high-value word, not to win individual letters at low cost. Bidding conservatively on every letter leaves me with coins but no letters.

When the opponent is bidding aggressively on a letter, I should recognize this signals the letter's value and either match them or concede strategically, depending on whether I need that letter for my word strategy.

When I have accumulated zero or one letter after several auction rounds, I've failed at the fundamental task. This means I was underbidding throughout. I should be winning letters, not preserving coins for a later round that never comes.

When evaluating a letter to bid on, I should think about which high-value words in the lexicon I could build, then work backward: if I want MASTER or STREAM (both worth 16 points when scored), I need M, A, S, T, E, and R. These are the letters I should actually compete for.

Before the auction starts, I should identify 2-3 target words I can realistically build, note which letters are essential for them, and bid to acquire those letters.

When bidding on early letters, I should bid more aggressively on the high-value and essential letters (M worth 3, plus the common letters needed for long words) and less on duplicates or less useful letters. But I must actually win letters in the early rounds—passive bidding in rounds 1-2 creates a deficit I cannot recover from.

I notice I bid 5 coins on both S and A in the first two rounds but still ended up with only S and A by the end. This means my opening bids were too high relative to my total budget and left me unable to compete for subsequent letters. I need to calibrate my opening bids lower so I can sustain competition across multiple letters.

My spending pattern showed I spent 5 coins to win S, then 5 coins (unsuccessfully) to win A, then had only 2 coins left. With 12 coins total and 8 letters, I should expect to spend roughly 1-2 coins per letter on average if I want to win 3-4 letters. Opening with a bid of 5 was too aggressive.

When I reach a point with very few coins remaining (like 2 coins with 3 letters left), I should recognize I've already lost the auction and should focus on whatever partial word I can form from my sparse letters.

When I have S and A and see T become available unsold after my opponent passes, taking T for 2 coins to form SAT is reasonable—it guarantees me a word worth 6 points (3 letters × 2 scoring). But I should never reach this state by poor bidding earlier.

When submitting a word at the end, I submit whatever word I can make from my letters. But I should have made sure I had letters that form a good word by bidding appropriately and more consistently throughout the auction.

My target strategy going forward: identify the 2-3 longest, highest-value words I can build, estimate which 4-5 letters are absolutely essential, and bid 1-3 coins on each essential letter in the early-to-middle rounds. Preserve 2-3 coins for late bidding if needed. Never spend more than 3 coins on a single low-value letter just because it's early.
